problem: Image-goal navigation methods rely on topological graphs, odometry, metric maps, RL in simulation or large amounts of passive video (NRNS uses 3.5M images), which makes them heavy and dependent on odometry in unseen scenes.
motivation: Humans navigate without detailed metric maps, so a lightweight memory and a decomposition of the task into scales should suffice. Feudal RL's hierarchy of managers and workers, each seeing different aspects at different spatial and temporal scales, suits navigation in unseen environments without distance-based rewards, so the paper adapts it to a no-RL setting.
key_idea: A no-RL, no-graph, no-odometry feudal hierarchy: a high-level manager keeps a self-supervised 2D latent map of visited areas, a mid-level manager trained on human point-click data predicts visible waypoints, and a low-level worker executes actions with SuperGlue matching.
insight: The latent map as input to the waypoint predictor is the biggest gain: the ablation raises curved-path average success from about 28-29 (no map) to 30.83 (FeudalNav) and 40.50 (Stacked) and straight SPL from about 22 to 37.7, because it encodes visit frequency and localizes the agent. Depth and 3 stacked frames alone change metrics little but qualitatively reduce collisions and circling. Stacking more history raises success but lowers SPL, reflecting over-exploration. SMoG gives the most distance-preserving latent space compared with MoCo, SwAV and ResNet features.
method: High-level manager (Latent Map): SMoG contrastive model trained with positive pairs from SuperGlue-based clustering of images per room; at test time features are clustered (MSE threshold α=300), projected to 2D with Isomap, and drawn as 3-channel colored circles whose size reflects visit counts

Mid-level manager (Direction net): ResNet-18 with a 7-channel input (RGBD + RGB latent map) fine-tuned to regress the human point-click pixel; Stacked variant uses the current and previous two RGBD-Map inputs

Low-level worker: maps the predicted point in a 3x2 image grid to turn-left/turn-right/forward (or turn+forward) actions; takes t=2 actions per waypoint, tracks the waypoint crop via SuperGlue, and acts randomly with ε=0.1

Goal-directed module: SuperGlue matches the goal image to the current view; if confidence exceeds β=0.7 the mean matched keypoint replaces the predicted waypoint, and the agent stops when the match is confident and depth at the matches is ≤1m

Human navigation dataset: 300 trajectories in Gibson and Matterport in Habitat, 103K point-click frames plus landmark annotations, with the mid-level model trained on a 117-trajectory subset (36,834 frames)

setting.backbone: SMoG encoder + ResNet-18 waypoint predictor (trained) with SuperGlue (pretrained matcher)
setting.training_data: Human point-click dataset, 117 trajectories / ~37K frames from Gibson/Matterport, different environments from test; SMoG trained self-supervised on the same data
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (480x640, 120° FOV) plus goal RGB image; no odometry

numbers.eval_set_note: NRNS protocol test set of ~6k start-goal pairs from 14 Gibson environments; straight paths, average over easy/medium/hard
numbers.extra: Straight trajectories; 500 action limit, 1m success radius; no odometry
numbers.evidence: Table 1, Straight, FeudalNav (Ours) Average Succ 47.57 SPL 38.41

numbers_note: Split labelled 'test' as previously unseen Gibson environments under the NRNS protocol. Ablation Table 2 lists straight FeudalNav average as 45.73/37.69, which equals NRNS w/ noise in Table 1 and conflicts with Table 1's 47.57/38.41; Table 1 values used.
results: On unseen Gibson image-goal with the NRNS protocol, Stacked FeudalNav reaches 50.17 straight and 40.50 curved average success, beating NRNS w/out noise (46.97 / 23.97). SPL is lower than NRNS on straight paths (38.41 vs 41.49) but higher on curved (15.83 vs 12.43), using ~37K training images vs 3.5M for NRNS.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation (Habitat Gibson); no real-robot test
SPL lower than NRNS on straight paths and Stacked variant over-explores
Relies on SuperGlue matching and hand-tuned thresholds, and excludes comparison to some recent methods deemed unfair
